Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: John, a 77-year-old African-American man, was born and raised in Nigeria before becoming a refugee during his youth. Now married with a long career as a software engineer, John has found himself increasingly entangled in a web of avoidance behaviors that stem from his traumatic past. His story begins not only with the harrowing experiences he faced decades ago but also with how these memories have shaped his current life. John’s most distressing triggers are commands and instructions, which remind him of the authority figures who issued orders during his time as a refugee. These triggers are so potent that even today, when John is given an instruction at work or by his wife, he immediately feels a wave of dread and anxiety. The fear and panic are often compounded by the visual memories that flood his mind—snapshots of moments from his past where authority figures were issuing commands that led to dire consequences. The trauma-related events he experienced in Nigeria have left him with vivid picture-like memories, each representing a moment frozen in time. These images flash through his mind, sometimes when he is out in public, but often even in the quiet comfort of his home. The emotionless recall of these moments exacerbates John’s distress; he can see and remember every detail as if it were happening to someone else, which further isolates him from both his past and present experiences. John has developed several maladaptive strategies to cope with these overwhelming memories and triggers. He avoids going out in public as much as possible, believing that being outside increases the likelihood of encountering situations or people who might remind him of his traumatic past. This avoidance extends even to social interactions; he actively avoids other people, finding solace only in isolation where he can control his environment. To further manage these intrusive memories and triggers, John keeps himself mentally occupied all the time—working long hours on software projects, engaging in complex puzzles, or listening to music. His mind must be engaged constantly to prevent the flood of disturbing images from overwhelming him. However, this constant mental distraction often leads to a numbing effect where he feels detached not only from his memories but also from his present reality. This dissociative feeling further reinforces his avoidance behaviors and heightens his sensitivity to triggers. When he does venture out or engage with others, the slightest hint of an authority command can send him spiraling back into those emotionally numb moments, reinforcing his belief that avoiding such situations is safer. John’s occupation as a software engineer often puts him in environments where instructions are common—both from colleagues and supervisors. This occupational setting has become particularly challenging for him. The fear of encountering these triggers at work leads John to overcompensate by staying isolated within his projects, further straining his professional relationships and causing tension with his team. The cumulative effect of these avoidance strategies and memory issues is a life that feels increasingly restricted and disconnected from the world around him. What frightened John most was the realization that he could not continue living in this state of constant vigilance and isolation without affecting both his work and marriage. What finally brought John to seek help was an incident at work where his inability to respond effectively to instructions led to a significant mistake on a project, causing considerable stress for himself and his team. This event made him realize that the patterns he had developed were no longer sustainable and were starting to have serious consequences in his daily life. John is most hopeful for relief from these overwhelming memories and triggers so that he can reclaim some sense of normalcy and connection with both his work and family. He hopes therapy will help him find a way to manage his symptoms without completely isolating himself, allowing him to live more fully again.
